The upcoming MacBook Ultra is going to be anything but cheap — and aside from the brand-new thinner design, OLED display, and touch capabilities, there's still the added cost pressure from rising memory pricing to consider. The latest report suggests its production costs could be pushed even higher.

Apple has historically preferred to bring in multiple suppliers for components in order to secure stable display supply and the best possible pricing, and the company had originally hoped to take the same approach with the MacBook Ultra. However, according to supply chain sources, Apple has ultimately decided to go with just a single display supplier…

Apple's product line currently has three display partners: Samsung, LG, and BOE. Of these, BOE currently only produces displays for the company's lower-tier products, while mid- to high-end screen orders are split between Samsung and LG.

The MacBook Ultra will feature Apple's most sophisticated display to date. Integrating two-stack tandem OLED with touch functionality into a large-sized panel suitable for a notebook computer is no easy feat, and the latest supply chain report indicates that Apple has decided to source the panel exclusively from Samsung.

According to The Elec, LG failed to meet Apple's requirements in terms of production volume.

Apple demanded mass production on a large-area substrate. Samsung Display responded with its 8.6-generation OLED production line, while LG Display is reportedly considering sticking with its existing 6-generation line. Although the 6-generation line can also be used for notebook OLED production, its substrate efficiency and capacity fall short of the 8.6-generation. Because of insufficient early-stage output, Apple ultimately chose Samsung Display as the sole supplier.

It seems LG is only able to produce limited quantities, and the logistical complexity of having two suppliers simply isn't worth it. LG is not expected to have a chance to supply displays for this flagship MacBook until at least 2029.

This clearly puts Samsung in a stronger position in panel price negotiations, which is expected to drive up Apple's production costs. The company will very likely pass the extra expenses on to consumers, much as it has been doing with rising memory costs.

Given how astronomically expensive the MacBook Ultra could be, how keen are you to consider an upgrade? Feel free to share your thoughts in the comments section.
